title: Investment Committee Process
summary: The Investment Committee Process explains how a PE firm turns diligence findings into an approved decision to deploy capital.
definition: The Investment Committee process is the sponsor's internal governance path for evaluating, challenging, approving, or rejecting a transaction.
whyItMatters: PE operators care because the IC memo becomes the first binding version of the investment thesis, value creation plan, downside case, and accountability model.
example: An IC may approve a platform investment only after the deal team proves the EBITDA bridge, diligence risks, management plan, debt capacity, and exit path are credible.

articleSections.title: Treat IC as a Mandate for Evidence and Accountability
body: The Investment Committee allocates more than purchase equity. It commits the firm's reputation, operating capacity, debt relationships, concentration limits, and time. Its mandate is to decide whether evidence supports an attractive risk-adjusted return under the fund's strategy, not whether the deal team has worked hard or won a competitive process. The committee makes assumptions visible, identifies what could permanently impair capital, and records why the firm is qualified to own this asset better than the next bidder.

Evidence should be tiered. Confirmed facts include contracted debt terms, audited results, customer records, and executed agreements. Supported estimates include QoE adjustments, market growth, price realization, and achievable synergies with clear methods. Open hypotheses include management capacity, cross-sell, or exit-multiple expansion that still require proof. The IC memo labels the tier and owner of each material assumption. Blending all three into one confident forecast creates false precision and makes post-close accountability impossible.

Decision rights and records preserve institutional discipline. The deal lead owns the integrated recommendation; functional diligence leaders own their findings; operating partners own the feasibility of the value plan; capital-markets professionals own financing assumptions; and IC members approve, reject, defer, or condition the investment. Conflicts and dissent should be documented, not edited into consensus. The final record becomes the first accountability baseline for the board, 100-day plan, and future review of whether returns came from insight, execution, market movement, or luck.
articleSections.callout: An IC approval is a capital-allocation decision with explicit evidence, conditions, owners, and reasons—not a vote of confidence in deal momentum.

articleSections.title: Underwrite Base, Downside, and Upside as Distinct Cases
body: The base case should represent the most probable executable plan, not the midpoint between optimism and fear. It begins with defensible normalized EBITDA, explicit organic assumptions, fully costed initiatives, debt terms, working-capital needs, and an exit multiple supported by likely buyers. The downside removes uncertain initiatives, stresses volume, margin, interest, and timing, and tests liquidity and covenant headroom. The upside isolates genuine optionality rather than improving every variable simultaneously. IC members should see which assumptions drive returns and which are merely decorative.

Consider a business acquired for $200 million at 10x $20 million of EBITDA using $100 million of debt and $100 million of equity. In the base case, EBITDA reaches $28 million, debt falls to $65 million, and a 10x exit produces $280 million of enterprise value and $215 million of equity proceeds, or 2.15x MOIC before fees. A downside of $22 million EBITDA, $85 million debt, and an 8.5x multiple yields $102 million of equity, roughly 1.02x. The case survives but produces little return.

The upside might reach $34 million EBITDA, $50 million debt, and an 11x exit, producing $324 million of equity proceeds or 3.24x MOIC. That result should not justify price unless its levers have evidence and capacity. Sensitivities should decompose the contribution from EBITDA growth, debt paydown, and multiple change; show timing effects on IRR; and identify covenant or liquidity breakpoints. If the base case requires both flawless execution and multiple expansion, it is functionally an upside case mislabeled for approval.

articleSections.title: Integrate Operating Diligence with the Value-Creation Case
body: Operating diligence asks whether the company can physically produce the model. It tests capacity, process stability, systems, data, talent, service levels, supplier exposure, capex, and management bandwidth. A $4 million margin opportunity is not underwritten merely because a benchmark suggests it exists. The case specifies the operational source, action, gross benefit, recurring cost, investment, owner, timing, dependencies, and measurement method. This prevents benchmark gaps from becoming EBITDA without an executable mechanism.

Commercial, financial, and operational findings must reconcile. If commercial diligence forecasts 12% growth, operations confirms that labor, facilities, implementation capacity, and working capital can support it. If QoE normalizes overtime as recurring, the productivity plan cannot add back the same cost as a future saving. If procurement savings depend on volume commitments, the downside model includes minimum purchases and concentration risk. The integrated bridge distinguishes market growth, price, volume, mix, productivity, sourcing, investment, and stranded cost so IC can challenge double counting.

Pre-close outputs should already resemble initiative charters. The operating partner identifies day-one controls, first-100-day validation tests, leadership decisions, and long-lead resources. Management reviews the case where confidentiality and timing permit, because an initiative without an executive owner remains a sponsor hypothesis. The decision gate asks whether the value plan is sufficiently evidenced, resourced, and sequenced to support the purchase price. Attractive theoretical upside does not compensate for an organization unable to absorb the change program.

articleSections.title: Challenge, Condition, and Exercise Decision Rights
body: Challenge works best when questions are assigned to assumptions rather than personalities. One member can own the customer case, another debt resilience, another management and execution, and another exit comparables. Pre-reads should highlight changes since the prior gate, unresolved issues, and requested decisions so meeting time is spent on judgment rather than discovery. The deal team answers with evidence or marks the point unresolved. A forceful narrative is not a substitute for a data source, sensitivity, reference call, or bounded post-close test.

IC may approve with conditions when a risk can be resolved before capital is irreversibly committed. Conditions might include a purchase-price adjustment, financing commitment, customer reference threshold, key-manager retention agreement, representation, insurance coverage, capex reserve, or completion of a technical test. Each condition needs an owner, deadline, objective satisfaction standard, and named authority to waive it. Broad instructions to 'get comfortable' invite deal momentum to dilute the original concern and obscure who accepted residual risk.

Kill discipline applies when core evidence breaks: normalized EBITDA is materially lower, customer loss invalidates growth, leverage leaves no downside cushion, management risk cannot be mitigated, or price requires unsupported upside. Sunk diligence cost and fear of losing the auction are irrelevant to prospective return. Deferral is appropriate when information can resolve uncertainty without changing strategic logic. Approval is appropriate only when remaining risks are understood, priced, and owned. The chair ensures the recorded decision matches the committee's actual conditions.

articleSections.title: Track the Thesis After Close and Through Exit
body: The final IC case should flow directly into the 100-day plan and board dashboard. Every material thesis lever receives a baseline, owner, milestone, and proof date; every accepted risk receives an early-warning indicator and mitigation. At day 30, management may validate data and decision rights; by day 100, the board confirms, revises, or rejects initiative economics; quarterly thereafter, the sponsor reconciles actual EBITDA, cash, leverage, and capability development to the approved case. This prevents the memo from becoming an archive after signing.

Post-close reviews should distinguish forecast error from execution error. Market contraction may invalidate a volume assumption; a delayed pricing pilot may indicate execution failure; a lower exit multiple may be market movement; poor data that concealed churn may reveal diligence weakness. The firm learns only when attribution is honest. If the $28 million base-case EBITDA falls to $25 million, the review identifies which bridge components failed, whether downside actions preserve covenant headroom, and whether resources should move to higher-confidence levers.

At exit, the IC record helps explain realized returns and remaining buyer upside. It shows which insights were correct, which conditions mattered, how management responded to risks, and whether value creation is durable. That evidence improves the sale narrative and the firm's future underwriting. The goal is not to prove the original committee infallible; it is to create a closed learning loop from screening through ownership. A disciplined IC process protects capital before close and compounds institutional judgment after the outcome is known.
